To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a framework for deriving security protocol specifications from simple basic components, we have developed a logic for proving properties of security protocols, and we have used the framework and the logic to prove security of the ISO-9798 challenge-response protocol.

we have: a) introduced a framework for deriving security protocol from basic building blocks, b) used this framework to derive a family of key establishment protocols, and c) proved the correctness of these derived protocols using a logical system that is an extension of an existing logic.

we have introduced a basic framework for the derivation of security protocols from simple components, we have proved correct the ISO-9798 key exchange protocol using this framework, and we have extended our previous security protocol logic to include preconditions and temporal properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with

two aspects of security protocols: (1) a framework for deriving protocols, which we believe is useful in the analysis of protocols and (2) an initial step toward associating formal derivations with protocol derivation.
the development of a formal method for the specification, design, and analysis of security protocols.
the following questions: How can we derive complex security protocols from simple components?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the security protocol is correct if and only if its derivation is correct.
the security of a protocol can be derived from its structure, and that the structure is derived from the protocol components.
we have a formal derivation of ISO-9798 from two simple building blocks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a framework for protocol derivation and a logic for protocol verification that can be used to prove the security of a large family of protocols.

the security of the family of station-to-station protocols can be derived by a small set of protocol transformations and refinements from the security of the Diffie-Helmann and challenge-response protocols.
we have developed a formal method for proving correctness and security of security protocols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a protocol derivation system can provide a formal foundation for reasoning about security protocols and that the logical formalization of such a system is feasible.
a simple set of basic protocols can be combined using a simple set of transformations to derive many of the most widely used security protocols.
the structure of the family of protocols can be derived by composing the security properties of its basic components.
